title: Time prepositions: in, for, ago and since
title_target: Jag har inte träffat henne på ett helt år.
goal: Say exactly when something happens and how long it lasts — and stop translating English "in" and "for" word for word.
bekal: *i*, *på* and *om* with lengths of time: *i två år*, *på två år*, *om två år*
last, next and every: *i fredags*, *på fredag*, *på fredagar*
wave: Go back to Unit 1: retell last weekend aloud with *i fredags*, *förra veckan* and *för … sedan*, then add one sentence about next weekend with *på lördag*.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Sommarschemat
dialogs.intro: It's April, and the café is quiet after the lunch rush. Maja, Dian's boss, sits down with a coffee and the summer schedule. She needs to know when Dian can work.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.text: Dian, har du två minuter? Jag gör sommarschemat just nu.
lines.id: Dian, do you have two minutes? I'm doing the summer schedule right now.
lines.literal: Dian, have you two minutes? I make summer-schedule-the just now.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Javisst. Redan nu? Det är bara april.
lines.literal: yes-certainly. already now? it is only April.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.text: Ja, men sommaren kommer om sju veckor, och då vill alla vara lediga samtidigt.
lines.id: Yes, but summer comes in seven weeks, and then everybody wants to be off at the same time.
lines.literal: yes, but summer-the comes in seven weeks, and then want all be free same-time.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Jag har kurs på kvällarna till mitten av juni, men sedan är jag ledig.
lines.id: I have class in the evenings until the middle of June, but after that I'm free.
lines.literal: I have course on evenings-the till middle-the of June, but then am I free.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.text: Bra. Kan du jobba heltid under juli?
lines.id: Good. Can you work full-time during July?
lines.literal: good. can you work full-time during July?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Ja, förutom första veckan. Min mamma kommer på besök i början av juli.
lines.id: Yes, except the first week. My mom is coming to visit at the beginning of July.
lines.literal: yes, except first week-the. my mom comes on visit in beginning-the of July.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.text: Vad roligt! När träffades ni senast?
lines.id: How nice! When did you last see each other?
lines.literal: what fun! when met-each-other you(pl) last?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: För ett år sedan. Jag har inte träffat henne på ett helt år.
lines.id: A year ago. I haven't seen her for a whole year.
lines.literal: for a year since. I have not met her on a whole year.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.text: Oj, det är länge. Hur länge stannar hon?
lines.id: Oh, that's a long time. How long is she staying?
lines.literal: oh, it is long. how long stays she?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: I tre veckor. Hon har aldrig varit i Europa förut.
lines.id: For three weeks. She's never been to Europe before.
lines.literal: in three weeks. she has never been in Europe before.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.text: Då tar du ledigt den första veckan och jobbar resten av juli?
lines.id: So you take the first week off and work the rest of July?
lines.literal: then take you free the first week-the and work rest-the of July?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Precis. Förresten, hur länge har du haft kaféet?
lines.id: Exactly. By the way, how long have you had the café?
lines.literal: exactly. by-the-way, how long have you had café-the?

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.text: Sedan 2019. Vi renoverade hela lokalen på tre veckor innan vi öppnade.
lines.id: Since 2019. We renovated the whole place in three weeks before we opened.
lines.literal: since 2019. we renovated whole premises-the on three weeks before we opened.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: På tre veckor? Det låter omöjligt!
lines.id: In three weeks? That sounds impossible!
lines.literal: on three weeks? it sounds impossible!

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.text: Nästan. Och jag har inte haft semester på fem år, så i sommar stänger vi i två veckor i augusti.
lines.id: Almost. And I haven't had a vacation for five years, so this summer we're closing for two weeks in August.
lines.literal: almost. and I have not had vacation on five years, so in summer close we in two weeks in August.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Det låter klokt. Jag mejlar mina datum till dig på måndag.
lines.id: Sounds wise. I'll email you my dates on Monday.
lines.literal: it sounds wise. I email my dates to you on Monday.

notes: **I tre veckor** — *i* + a length of time answers the question *hur länge?* (how long?) and corresponds to English "for": *Hon stannar **i** tre veckor*, *Jag bodde i Lappis **i** ett år*. It works in the past, present and future alike. In relaxed speech Swedes often drop the *i* altogether — *Hon stannar tre veckor* — just as English speakers say "She's staying three weeks".

**På ett helt år** — here English "for" becomes *på*, not *i*. The trigger is the negation: when something **hasn't** happened for a period, Swedish uses *på*. *Jag har **inte** träffat henne **på** ett år*, *Vi har **inte** haft semester **på** fem år*. The most common version is a fixed phrase you will hear daily: *Vi har inte setts **på länge**!* (Long time no see!) — **poh LENG-eh**.

**Om sju veckor** — *om* + a length of time means "in" counted **from now** into the future: *om sju veckor*, *om en kvart*, *om två år*. Compare *på tre veckor* in Maja's later line, which means "in" as in **taking** three weeks to finish something. English uses one word, "in", for both; Swedish splits them, and mixing them up is one of the most common A2 mistakes.

**För ett år sedan** — "a year ago" needs both halves of the frame: *för … sedan*. On its own, **sedan** has two more jobs in this dialogue: "since" (*sedan 2019*) and "then, after that" (*men sedan är jag ledig*). In speech all three are pronounced **sen**, and in texts and chat you will see it spelled *sen* too: *för ett år sen*, *sen 2019*.

**Under juli** — *under* means "during" and stresses the whole stretch of time: *under juli*, *under kursen*, *under sommaren*. You could also say *i juli*, which simply places something in that month. The literal meaning "under, below" lives on as well: *katten ligger under bordet*. Context sorts it out.

**I början av / i mitten av / i slutet av** — at the beginning / in the middle / at the end of. Learn them as three ready-made frames: *i början av juli*, *i mitten av juni*, *i slutet av augusti*. Note *början* (**BÖR-yahn**): the *rj* is said as "ry", and the word has no other form — it only ever appears like this. And **förresten** (**fö-RES-ten**), "by the way", is how Swedes change the subject politely.

grammars.title: "In" and "for": which Swedish word?
body: English gets by with two little words, "in" and "for". Swedish needs five, depending on the question you are really answering. Read the table across: the English column is where the trap is.

head: English
Swedish
Question it answers
Example
rows: Jag bodde i Lappis **i** ett år.
How long since it last happened?
Jag har inte sett honom **på** länge.
Hon lärde sig cykla **på** en vecka.

after: The single most useful pair to memorize: *Jag läste **i** två år* (I studied for two years — that's how long it lasted) vs *Jag lärde mig svenska **på** två år* (I learned Swedish in two years — that's how long it took to get there).

With *sedan* (since) Swedish normally uses the **perfect**, just like English: *Jag **har** bott här sedan i höstas*. But *för … sedan* (ago) takes the **simple past**, again just like English: *Jag **flyttade** hit för två år sedan*. Here, for once, the two languages agree.

grammars.title: Last, next and every
body: For days of the week, seasons and holidays, Swedish shows past, future or habit through tiny changes in the preposition and the ending. The past forms with *-s* (*i fredags*, *i somras*) look odd, but they are among the most frequent expressions in the language.
after: **Months** take *i*: *i juli*, *i augusti*. **Years** usually take no preposition at all: *Hon föddes 1998*, *Vi öppnade 2019* (in writing also *år 2019*). **Decades and centuries** take *på*: *på 90-talet* (in the nineties), *på 1800-talet* (in the 1800s).

**How often:** *en gång **i** veckan*, *två gånger **i** månaden* — but *tre gånger **om** dagen*, *en gång **om** året*. Day and year take *om*; week and month take *i*. There's no deep logic; it just sounds right to Swedish ears.

head: English sentence
Wrong (word for word)
Right
rows: I've lived here for two years.
Jag har bott här för två år.
Jag har bott här **i** två år.
I haven't slept for two days.
Jag har inte sovit i två dagar.
Jag har inte sovit **på** två dagar.
She wrote the essay in one night.
Hon skrev uppsatsen om en natt.
I moved here two years ago.
Jag flyttade hit två år sedan.

blocks.text: The second row is worth a closer look: *Vi ses i en vecka* is not just wrong — it means something else, "we'll be seeing each other for a week". That is why the choice matters: the wrong little word does not only sound foreign, it can change the message.

**Klockan** and **vid**: for clock times you say *klockan åtta* (at eight), often written *kl. 8*. For a rough time, Swedes add *-tiden* and use *vid*: ***vid** åttatiden* (around eight), ***vid** lunchtid* (around lunchtime). *Vid* also works for big holidays: *vid jul* (around Christmas).

blocks.title: Spiral review — back to Unit 2
items: *Till* is a preposition (followed by a noun or a time): *till juni*, *till mitten av juni*.
*Tills* is a linking word from Unit 2 (followed by a whole clause): *Jag jobbar **tills** kursen slutar*.
Same pair in English: "until June" vs "until the course ends". English uses one word; Swedish adds an *-s* when a clause follows.

blocks.text: Note the false friend: Swedish **semester** means a **vacation** from work, not half of an academic year. The university half-year is *en termin*. *Jag har semester i juli* = I'm on vacation in July.

By law, everyone working in Sweden has the right to **25 days** of paid vacation a year, and to **four weeks in a row** during the summer months. The result is that much of the country goes quiet in July: offices slow down, some small shops and cafés close, and Stockholmers head for their summer cottages. That's why Maja plans the summer schedule as early as April.
